title: Microbial Biochemistry
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 300L Microbial Biochemistry curriculum: enzyme structure/kinetics, bioenergetics, central carbon metabolism (glycolysis, TCA cycle, electron transport, chemiosmosis), fermentation pathways, autotrophic metabolism, nitrogen metabolism, and biosynthesis/regulation of macromolecules in microorganisms.

questions.question: Enzymes increase the rate of biochemical reactions mainly by:
options: Increasing the free energy of the products
Lowering the activation energy required for the reaction to proceed
Shifting the equilibrium constant of the reaction
Increasing the temperature of the reaction mixture
questions.correct_answer: Lowering the activation energy required for the reaction to proceed
questions.explanation: Enzymes act as biological catalysts by stabilising the transition state, thereby lowering the activation energy needed for substrate to be converted to product, without changing the reaction's overall free energy change or equilibrium.

questions.question: In Michaelis-Menten enzyme kinetics, Km (the Michaelis constant) represents:
options: The substrate concentration at which reaction velocity is half of Vmax
The total amount of enzyme present
The number of active sites per enzyme molecule
questions.correct_answer: The substrate concentration at which reaction velocity is half of Vmax
questions.explanation: Km is defined as the substrate concentration at which the reaction proceeds at half its maximum velocity (Vmax/2) and is a measure of an enzyme's affinity for its substrate: a low Km indicates high affinity.

questions.question: A competitive enzyme inhibitor typically:
options: Binds the active site and can be overcome by increasing substrate concentration, raising apparent Km while Vmax stays unchanged
Binds only to the enzyme-substrate complex and lowers Vmax without affecting Km
Permanently destroys the enzyme's active site
Increases the enzyme's affinity for substrate
questions.correct_answer: Binds the active site and can be overcome by increasing substrate concentration, raising apparent Km while Vmax stays unchanged
questions.explanation: Competitive inhibitors compete with substrate for the active site; because the inhibition can be outcompeted by excess substrate, Vmax remains achievable but a higher substrate concentration is needed, so apparent Km increases while Vmax is unchanged.

questions.question: Allosteric enzymes, which are often the target of feedback inhibition in biosynthetic pathways, are characterised by:
options: Having only one substrate-binding site that also binds regulatory molecules
Binding regulatory effector molecules at a site distinct from the active site, altering enzyme activity through conformational change
Being unaffected by any small-molecule regulators
questions.correct_answer: Binding regulatory effector molecules at a site distinct from the active site, altering enzyme activity through conformational change
questions.explanation: Allosteric enzymes possess a regulatory (allosteric) site separate from the catalytic site; binding of an effector there changes the enzyme's conformation and activity, a mechanism commonly used in end-product feedback inhibition.

questions.question: In feedback (end-product) inhibition of a microbial biosynthetic pathway, the final product of the pathway typically:
options: Activates the first enzyme of the pathway
Inhibits an early, often the first, enzyme of its own biosynthetic pathway
Has no effect on any enzyme in the pathway
Only inhibits enzymes in unrelated pathways
questions.correct_answer: Inhibits an early, often the first, enzyme of its own biosynthetic pathway
questions.explanation: Feedback inhibition allows a cell to conserve resources: accumulation of the pathway's end product allosterically inhibits an early committed enzyme in the same pathway, throttling further synthesis when enough product is present.

questions.question: The overall process by which cells extract energy from nutrients and use it to drive energy-requiring reactions is termed:
questions.correct_answer: Bioenergetics/metabolism
questions.explanation: Metabolism (bioenergetics) encompasses all the chemical reactions of a cell, including catabolism (energy-yielding breakdown) and anabolism (energy-requiring synthesis).

questions.question: ATP is often called the 'energy currency' of the cell because:
options: It cannot be synthesised by microorganisms
Hydrolysis of its terminal phosphoanhydride bond releases free energy that is readily coupled to drive endergonic cellular reactions
It is the only molecule that can cross the plasma membrane
It is the final electron acceptor in all metabolic pathways
questions.correct_answer: Hydrolysis of its terminal phosphoanhydride bond releases free energy that is readily coupled to drive endergonic cellular reactions
questions.explanation: ATP's high-energy phosphoanhydride bonds release substantial free energy on hydrolysis to ADP + Pi, and this energy is enzymatically coupled to power biosynthesis, transport, and motility.

questions.question: During glycolysis, one molecule of glucose is broken down to yield a net of:
questions.correct_answer: 2 pyruvate, net 2 ATP, and 2 NADH
questions.explanation: Glycolysis converts one glucose into two pyruvate molecules, with a net gain of 2 ATP (4 produced minus 2 invested) and 2 NADH per glucose, occurring in the cytoplasm of both prokaryotes and eukaryotes.

questions.question: Substrate-level phosphorylation, as occurs during glycolysis, refers to:
options: ATP synthesis driven directly by transfer of a phosphate group from a high-energy metabolic intermediate to ADP
ATP synthesis driven by the proton motive force across a membrane
Phosphorylation of glucose by hexokinase only
ATP breakdown to release energy for muscle contraction
questions.correct_answer: ATP synthesis driven directly by transfer of a phosphate group from a high-energy metabolic intermediate to ADP
questions.explanation: Substrate-level phosphorylation generates ATP by direct enzymatic transfer of a phosphate group from a high-energy substrate (e.g. 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate, phosphoenolpyruvate) to ADP, distinct from membrane-based oxidative phosphorylation.

questions.question: Before entering the tricarboxylic acid (TCA/Krebs) cycle, pyruvate produced by glycolysis is first converted to:
options: Acetyl-CoA, via the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, releasing CO2 and generating NADH
questions.correct_answer: Acetyl-CoA, via the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, releasing CO2 and generating NADH
questions.explanation: The multienzyme pyruvate dehydrogenase complex oxidatively decarboxylates pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, releasing one CO2 and reducing NAD+ to NADH, linking glycolysis to the TCA cycle.

questions.question: One complete turn of the TCA cycle, starting from acetyl-CoA, directly produces:
options: 2 NADH, 2 FADH2, 2 ATP, and no CO2
questions.correct_answer: 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, 1 GTP/ATP, and 2 CO2
questions.explanation: Each turn of the TCA cycle oxidises the two carbons of acetyl-CoA fully to CO2, generating 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, and 1 GTP (or ATP) by substrate-level phosphorylation, which together feed further ATP production via the electron transport chain.

questions.question: In the electron transport chain (ETC) of aerobic respiration, the terminal electron acceptor is:
questions.correct_answer: Oxygen
questions.explanation: In aerobic respiration, electrons passed along the ETC carriers are ultimately accepted by molecular oxygen, which is reduced to water; this is what distinguishes aerobic respiration from anaerobic respiration and fermentation.

questions.question: The chemiosmotic hypothesis explains ATP synthesis during oxidative phosphorylation as resulting from:
options: Direct transfer of phosphate from ETC carriers to ADP
A proton gradient (proton motive force) generated across a membrane by electron transport, which drives ATP synthase to phosphorylate ADP
Simple diffusion of ATP across the membrane
Conversion of NADH directly into ATP without any intermediate steps
questions.correct_answer: A proton gradient (proton motive force) generated across a membrane by electron transport, which drives ATP synthase to phosphorylate ADP
questions.explanation: As electrons flow through the ETC, protons are pumped across the membrane, creating an electrochemical (proton motive) gradient; the flow of protons back through ATP synthase drives ATP synthesis, as proposed in Peter Mitchell's chemiosmotic theory.

questions.question: In bacteria, unlike in eukaryotic mitochondria, the electron transport chain and ATP synthase are located in the:
questions.correct_answer: Plasma (cytoplasmic) membrane
questions.explanation: Bacteria lack mitochondria, so the electron transport chain components and ATP synthase are embedded in the plasma membrane, which functions analogously to the inner mitochondrial membrane.

questions.question: Anaerobic respiration differs from aerobic respiration in that it:
options: Uses no electron transport chain at all
Uses an electron transport chain but with a terminal electron acceptor other than oxygen, such as nitrate, sulfate, or fumarate
questions.correct_answer: Uses an electron transport chain but with a terminal electron acceptor other than oxygen, such as nitrate, sulfate, or fumarate
questions.explanation: Anaerobic respiration still uses an electron transport chain and chemiosmosis to generate ATP, but substitutes an alternative terminal electron acceptor (e.g. NO3-, SO4^2-, CO2) for oxygen, typically yielding less ATP per glucose than aerobic respiration.

questions.question: Fermentation is distinguished from respiration in that fermentation:
options: Uses an external inorganic terminal electron acceptor
Uses an organic molecule (often a product of the pathway itself, such as pyruvate) as the terminal electron acceptor, regenerating NAD+ without an electron transport chain
Always produces more ATP per glucose than aerobic respiration
questions.correct_answer: Uses an organic molecule (often a product of the pathway itself, such as pyruvate) as the terminal electron acceptor, regenerating NAD+ without an electron transport chain
questions.explanation: Fermentation regenerates NAD+ from NADH by transferring electrons to an organic acceptor (e.g. pyruvate to lactate, or acetaldehyde to ethanol) without an electron transport chain, yielding far less ATP (via substrate-level phosphorylation only) than respiration.

questions.question: In homolactic fermentation, as performed by Lactobacillus species, pyruvate is reduced directly to:
questions.correct_answer: Lactate, with no CO2 released
questions.explanation: Homolactic fermenters convert pyruvate essentially quantitatively to lactate via lactate dehydrogenase, regenerating NAD+, with lactic acid as virtually the sole end product and no CO2 evolved.

questions.question: In alcoholic fermentation carried out by Saccharomyces cerevisiae, pyruvate is first decarboxylated to acetaldehyde, which is then reduced to:
options: Ethanol, by alcohol dehydrogenase, regenerating NAD+
questions.correct_answer: Ethanol, by alcohol dehydrogenase, regenerating NAD+
questions.explanation: Yeast pyruvate decarboxylase converts pyruvate to acetaldehyde and CO2; alcohol dehydrogenase then reduces acetaldehyde to ethanol using NADH, regenerating NAD+ needed to sustain glycolysis.

questions.question: The pentose phosphate pathway is important to microbial metabolism mainly because it generates:
options: ATP only, with no other products
NADPH for biosynthetic reductive reactions and ribose-5-phosphate for nucleotide biosynthesis
questions.correct_answer: NADPH for biosynthetic reductive reactions and ribose-5-phosphate for nucleotide biosynthesis
questions.explanation: The pentose phosphate pathway is primarily biosynthetic, supplying NADPH (used in reductive biosynthesis and antioxidant defence) and ribose-5-phosphate (a precursor for nucleotides and nucleic acids), rather than being a major ATP generator.

questions.question: The Entner-Doudoroff pathway, found in certain bacteria such as Pseudomonas and Zymomonas as an alternative to glycolysis, characteristically yields:
options: 2 ATP, 2 NADH and 2 NADPH per glucose, the same as classical glycolysis
Only 1 net ATP per glucose (compared with the 2 net ATP of the Embden-Meyerhof pathway), along with NADPH and NADH
Only CO2 and water as products
questions.correct_answer: Only 1 net ATP per glucose (compared with the 2 net ATP of the Embden-Meyerhof pathway), along with NADPH and NADH
questions.explanation: The Entner-Doudoroff pathway converts glucose to pyruvate via a distinct route using key intermediates such as 6-phosphogluconate and 2-keto-3-deoxy-6-phosphogluconate, yielding only 1 net ATP per glucose (less than glycolysis) plus one NADPH and one NADH.

questions.question: Chemolithotrophic bacteria such as Nitrosomonas obtain energy by:
options: Oxidising inorganic compounds such as ammonia, and using the released energy to fix carbon dioxide
Direct absorption of ATP from the environment
questions.correct_answer: Oxidising inorganic compounds such as ammonia, and using the released energy to fix carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Chemolithotrophs derive energy by oxidising inorganic electron donors (e.g. NH3, NH4+, H2S, Fe2+); Nitrosomonas specifically oxidises ammonia to nitrite, coupling this oxidation to ATP generation and CO2 fixation.

questions.question: In oxygenic photosynthesis performed by cyanobacteria, the source of electrons used to reduce NADP+ and the source of the oxygen released are both:
questions.correct_answer: Water
questions.explanation: Cyanobacteria, like plants, use photosystem II to split water, releasing O2 as a byproduct and supplying electrons that are ultimately used, via photosystem I, to reduce NADP+ to NADPH.

questions.question: Purple and green sulfur bacteria perform anoxygenic photosynthesis using electron donors such as:
options: Water, releasing oxygen as in plants
Hydrogen sulfide (H2S) or other reduced sulfur compounds, without producing oxygen
questions.correct_answer: Hydrogen sulfide (H2S) or other reduced sulfur compounds, without producing oxygen
questions.explanation: Anoxygenic phototrophic bacteria use reduced compounds such as H2S (often depositing elemental sulfur) rather than water as the electron donor for photosynthesis, and consequently do not evolve oxygen.

questions.question: Biological nitrogen fixation, the conversion of atmospheric N2 to ammonia, is catalysed by the enzyme complex:
questions.correct_answer: Nitrogenase
questions.explanation: Nitrogenase, found in diazotrophic prokaryotes such as Rhizobium and Azotobacter, catalyses the highly energy-demanding reduction of atmospheric N2 to NH3, and is extremely sensitive to inactivation by oxygen.

questions.question: Nitrification, the two-step microbial oxidation of ammonia to nitrate in soil and water, involves ammonia oxidation to nitrite followed by:
options: Reduction of nitrite back to ammonia
Oxidation of nitrite to nitrate, typically by bacteria such as Nitrobacter
Reduction of nitrite to nitrogen gas
Conversion of nitrite directly to organic nitrogen
questions.correct_answer: Oxidation of nitrite to nitrate, typically by bacteria such as Nitrobacter
questions.explanation: Nitrification proceeds in two stages performed by different chemolithotrophic genera: ammonia-oxidisers (e.g. Nitrosomonas) convert NH3 to nitrite, and nitrite-oxidisers (e.g. Nitrobacter) then oxidise nitrite to nitrate.

questions.question: Denitrification, an important process in the nitrogen cycle carried out by bacteria such as Pseudomonas denitrificans, is defined as the:
options: Fixation of atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia
Reduction of nitrate stepwise to nitrogen gas (or nitrous oxide), used as an anaerobic respiratory pathway
Assimilation of nitrate into amino acids
questions.correct_answer: Reduction of nitrate stepwise to nitrogen gas (or nitrous oxide), used as an anaerobic respiratory pathway
questions.explanation: Denitrifying bacteria use nitrate (and its reduction intermediates) as terminal electron acceptors in anaerobic respiration, ultimately releasing N2 (or N2O) gas back to the atmosphere and completing the nitrogen cycle.

questions.question: The building blocks (monomer units) used for peptidoglycan biosynthesis in the bacterial cell wall are:
options: N-acetylglucosamine (NAG) and N-acetylmuramic acid (NAM), cross-linked by short peptide chains
questions.correct_answer: N-acetylglucosamine (NAG) and N-acetylmuramic acid (NAM), cross-linked by short peptide chains
questions.explanation: Peptidoglycan is a polymer of alternating NAG and NAM sugar residues linked by beta-1,4 glycosidic bonds, with adjacent glycan strands cross-linked by short peptide chains attached to NAM, giving the wall its rigidity.

questions.question: Fatty acid biosynthesis in bacteria proceeds mainly by the stepwise, two-carbon-at-a-time addition of acetyl units, using which activated carrier molecule as the two-carbon donor for chain elongation?
options: Acetyl-CoA condensed via malonyl-CoA, formed by carboxylation of acetyl-CoA
questions.correct_answer: Acetyl-CoA condensed via malonyl-CoA, formed by carboxylation of acetyl-CoA
questions.explanation: Fatty acid synthase elongates the growing acyl chain by repeatedly condensing it with malonyl-CoA (formed by carboxylating acetyl-CoA via acetyl-CoA carboxylase), releasing CO2 at each condensation and adding two carbons per cycle.

questions.question: Amino acids are classified as essential in an organism when they:
options: Are needed only in trace amounts
Cannot be synthesised by the organism and must be obtained from an external (dietary/environmental) source
Are exclusively used to build nucleic acids
Are synthesised in unlimited quantity by all organisms
questions.correct_answer: Cannot be synthesised by the organism and must be obtained from an external (dietary/environmental) source
questions.explanation: Essential amino acids are those an organism lacks the biosynthetic pathway to make itself, so they must be supplied exogenously; many microorganisms, unlike humans, can synthesise all 20 amino acids de novo from simpler precursors.

questions.question: Transamination reactions in amino acid metabolism involve:
options: Transfer of an amino group from one amino acid to an alpha-keto acid, forming a new amino acid and a new keto acid, catalysed by transaminases (aminotransferases)
Irreversible destruction of the amino acid's carbon skeleton
Direct conversion of amino acids into fatty acids
questions.correct_answer: Transfer of an amino group from one amino acid to an alpha-keto acid, forming a new amino acid and a new keto acid, catalysed by transaminases (aminotransferases)
questions.explanation: Transamination, catalysed by pyridoxal-phosphate-dependent aminotransferases, interconverts amino acids and keto acids by shuttling amino groups, a key step in both amino acid synthesis and degradation.

questions.question: Oxidative deamination of glutamate by glutamate dehydrogenase releases nitrogen in the form of:
questions.correct_answer: Free ammonia (NH3/NH4+), while regenerating alpha-ketoglutarate
questions.explanation: Glutamate dehydrogenase removes the amino group from glutamate as free ammonia, regenerating alpha-ketoglutarate, a key TCA cycle intermediate, and linking amino acid catabolism to central carbon metabolism.

questions.question: Purine and pyrimidine nucleotide biosynthesis in microorganisms requires which class of molecule as the carbon/nitrogen skeleton precursor for the ring structures?
options: Amino acids (e.g. glycine, glutamine, aspartate), together with CO2 and one-carbon units
questions.correct_answer: Amino acids (e.g. glycine, glutamine, aspartate), together with CO2 and one-carbon units
questions.explanation: The purine and pyrimidine rings are built up from small precursors including the amino acids glycine, glutamine and aspartate, along with CO2 and one-carbon units donated by tetrahydrofolate derivatives.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes catabolism from anabolism?
options: Catabolism is energy-releasing (exergonic) breakdown of complex molecules; anabolism is energy-requiring (endergonic) synthesis of complex molecules from simpler ones
Catabolism only occurs in anaerobes, while anabolism only occurs in aerobes
Catabolism builds macromolecules while anabolism degrades them
There is no meaningful biochemical distinction between the two
questions.correct_answer: Catabolism is energy-releasing (exergonic) breakdown of complex molecules; anabolism is energy-requiring (endergonic) synthesis of complex molecules from simpler ones
questions.explanation: Catabolic pathways break down nutrients to release free energy (often captured as ATP and reducing power), while anabolic pathways use that energy to build complex cellular components from simpler precursors.

questions.question: Amphibolic pathways, such as the TCA cycle, are so named because they:
options: Serve both catabolic (energy-generating) and anabolic (biosynthetic precursor-supplying) roles
questions.correct_answer: Serve both catabolic (energy-generating) and anabolic (biosynthetic precursor-supplying) roles
questions.explanation: The TCA cycle both oxidises acetyl-CoA to generate reducing equivalents and ATP (catabolic role) and supplies intermediates such as oxaloacetate and alpha-ketoglutarate as precursors for amino acid and other biosyntheses (anabolic role), making it amphibolic.

questions.question: Anaplerotic reactions, such as that catalysed by pyruvate carboxylase, function to:
options: Replenish TCA cycle intermediates that have been withdrawn for biosynthesis
Break down TCA cycle intermediates completely to CO2
questions.correct_answer: Replenish TCA cycle intermediates that have been withdrawn for biosynthesis
questions.explanation: When TCA intermediates are drawn off for biosynthesis (e.g. oxaloacetate for amino acids), anaplerotic reactions such as carboxylation of pyruvate to oxaloacetate replenish the pool, keeping the cycle running.

questions.question: The glyoxylate cycle, present in many bacteria and fungi but absent in humans, allows microorganisms to:
options: Grow using two-carbon compounds such as acetate as the sole carbon source, by bypassing the CO2-releasing steps of the TCA cycle
questions.correct_answer: Grow using two-carbon compounds such as acetate as the sole carbon source, by bypassing the CO2-releasing steps of the TCA cycle
questions.explanation: The glyoxylate cycle uses isocitrate lyase and malate synthase to bypass the two decarboxylation steps of the TCA cycle, allowing net synthesis of four-carbon compounds from two-carbon acetyl-CoA units, enabling growth on acetate or fatty acids.

questions.question: A microorganism that can synthesise all its required organic cellular constituents from CO2 as the sole carbon source is described as:
questions.correct_answer: Autotrophic
questions.explanation: Autotrophs (whether photoautotrophic or chemoautotrophic) use CO2 as their carbon source, fixing it into organic molecules, in contrast to heterotrophs, which require pre-formed organic carbon compounds.
